title: AI-Based Detection and Classification of Industrial Fires and Persistent Thermal Sources Using NASA FIRMS, OSM & Satellite Data
description:
• Background Industrial facilities generate thermal signatures that can be observed from space, but current satellite-based monitoring systems like NASA FIRMS cannot distinguish between different types of thermal anomalies. To address this, there is a challenge to develop an AI-enabled geospatial system that integrates thermal data, land-cover information, industrial databases, and satellite imagery to automatically identify, classify, and monitor industrial fires and persistent thermal sources.
• Description Industrial facilities such as oil refineries, petrochemical complexes, thermal power plants, steel industries, mining areas, and LNG terminals generate thermal signatures that can be observed from space. In addition, accidental industrial fires, gas leaks, explosions, and abnormal thermal events pose significant risks to critical infrastructure, public safety, and the environment.
Current satellite-based fire monitoring systems such as NASA FIRMS provide thermal anomaly detections but do not distinguish between industrial fires, gas flares, agricultural burning, mining activity, and wildfires.
The challenge is to develop an AI-enabled geospatial system that can automatically identify, classify, and monitor industrial fires and persistent thermal sources by integrating thermal anomaly data, land-cover information, industrial infrastructure databases, and satellite imagery.
• Expected Solution/Deliverables:
i. Classification and segregation of Industrial fires from forest fires and other natural fires.
ii. GIS based solution for data storage, visualization of the output as an overlay over maps
summary: Innovation (5/5): draws on ai, satellite, gis applied to a miscellaneous problem, placing it in the breakthrough band. Feasibility (4/5): as a software build with moderate integration complexity, a working prototype is realistic in a 36-hour window. Impact (3/5): addresses a more targeted user group within Miscellaneous. Tech Depth (4/5): centers on gis, infrastructure. Sustainability (3/5): will need a maintenance/upkeep plan post-hackathon. Scalability (2/5): currently scoped narrowly and would need rework to scale. Total 21/30 -> Green verdict.

detail.title: AI-Based Detection and Classification of Industrial Fires and Persistent Thermal Sources Using NASA FIRMS, OSM & Satellite Data

overview.in_plain_terms: Build a system that takes NASA's raw thermal anomaly detections and automatically figures out what they actually are, an industrial fire, a routine gas flare, agricultural burning, or a wildfire, by combining that thermal signal with land-use maps and industrial facility databases.
overview.why_it_matters: NASA FIRMS currently flags thermal anomalies but can't tell you what caused them. Adding that classification layer turns raw satellite data into genuinely actionable intelligence for critical infrastructure monitoring.
pain_points: NASA FIRMS and similar systems detect thermal anomalies but can't distinguish their cause.
Industrial fires, gas flares, agricultural burning, mining activity, and wildfires all produce similar raw thermal signatures.
No integrated system combines thermal data with land-cover and industrial-facility context for automatic classification.
overview.background: Satellite thermal anomaly detection (NASA FIRMS) identifies heat signatures but can't distinguish industrial fires from gas flares, agricultural burning, or wildfires, limiting its usefulness for critical infrastructure monitoring.
overview.whats_being_asked: An AI-enabled geospatial system integrating NASA FIRMS thermal data, OpenStreetMap land-cover/industrial data, and satellite imagery to automatically classify thermal anomaly types.
expected_solution: NASA FIRMS thermal anomaly data ingestion.
OSM/industrial database integration for spatial context.
AI-based classification of thermal source type (industrial fire, flare, agricultural burn, mining, wildfire).
Monitoring dashboard for critical infrastructure thermal events.

analysis.innovation_scope_note: Breakthrough. Genuine multi-source fusion (thermal data plus land-cover plus industrial context) for thermal-source classification is a real, valuable, technically substantial application.
analysis.invention_effort_note: Moderate-high. NASA FIRMS and OSM data are both genuinely public and accessible; real effort is in the classification logic combining spatial context with thermal characteristics.

competitive_landscape.note: Genuinely achievable with real public data sources, a specialized but accessible combination for a team with GIS/classification skill.

innovation.note: Genuine multi-source fusion for thermal-source classification addresses a real, explicitly-named gap in existing tools.

invention.note: Combining thermal, land-cover, and industrial-facility data into coherent classification logic is real, substantial integration work.

technical_feasibility.note: NASA FIRMS thermal data and OpenStreetMap data are both genuinely public and directly accessible, a real data advantage.

impact_and_benefits.note: Directly improves monitoring capability for real industrial safety and critical infrastructure risk.

architecture.note: Multi-source data fusion feeding a classification model, well-understood pattern with genuinely accessible real data.

overall_verdict.reasoning: Strong pick, one of the higher-scoring PS in this batch, and genuinely achievable given real, accessible public data (NASA FIRMS and OSM both directly usable). This is one of the better-resourced PS in the entire dataset for real data access.

evaluator_lens.biggest_strength: Both core data sources (NASA FIRMS thermal detections, OpenStreetMap industrial/land-cover data) are genuinely public and directly usable, a real, significant data advantage.
evaluator_lens.biggest_risk: Building classification without genuine spatial correlation logic (just labeling thermal points by nearest OSM feature naively) would miss real classification nuance, like distinguishing an actual fire event from a facility's normal operational flare.
evaluator_lens.validate_before_commit: Test your classification logic against genuinely ambiguous cases, a thermal detection near an industrial facility that could be either routine flaring or an actual fire event, and design features that genuinely discriminate between these, not just proximity matching.

idea_0_4: Source real NASA FIRMS thermal anomaly data and OpenStreetMap industrial/land-cover data for a test region.
Design your classification feature set combining thermal characteristics (intensity, persistence, size) with spatial context.
Split: one person on data integration/fusion, one on the classification model.
prototype_4_22: Build your multi-source data ingestion and spatial correlation pipeline.
Build your classification model distinguishing thermal source types.
Test against known real thermal events near identifiable industrial facilities in your test region.
integration_22_30: Refine classification based on discrimination test results, especially genuinely ambiguous cases.
Build the monitoring dashboard showing classified thermal events on a map.
Add persistence tracking (distinguishing a one-off event from a recurring/persistent thermal source).
polish_30_36: Polish the dashboard for genuine monitoring-analyst usability.
Rehearse a live demo showing real thermal detections correctly classified against real industrial context.
Prepare to discuss how your model handles genuinely ambiguous classification cases.
build_plan.how_to_stand_out: Show your system correctly classifying a real, genuinely ambiguous thermal detection, distinguishing a routine gas flare from what could be an actual fire event near the same facility, using real NASA FIRMS and OSM data, that discrimination on real, tricky cases is the actual hard, differentiating value here.

strengths: Both core data sources are genuinely public and directly accessible, a significant real-data advantage.
Addresses a real, explicitly-named gap in existing satellite monitoring tools.
weaknesses: Genuine discrimination between similar thermal source types (flare vs. fire) needs careful feature design, not just proximity matching.
Ground-truth labels for training/validation (confirmed fire vs. flare events) may be limited.

team_fit.ideal_ratio: Balanced, with real GIS skill for the spatial correlation work.
team_fit.approach: Source and explore real FIRMS/OSM data early, this genuine data access is a real strength to build on quickly.

ai_buildability_split.ai_can_build_fast: Standard classification model scaffolding and data-fusion pipeline.
ai_buildability_split.needs_human_judgment: Designing features that genuinely discriminate between similar thermal source types (not just proximity to an industrial facility), that requires real domain understanding of industrial thermal signatures.
ai_buildability_split.risk_of_leaning_on_ai_only: A classifier based only on naive proximity to OSM features (nearest industrial facility = industrial fire) would miss real discrimination nuance and likely misclassify routine operational events as anomalies.

data_resource_availability.status: NASA FIRMS thermal data and OpenStreetMap data are both genuinely public and directly accessible, a strong real-data foundation.
data_resource_availability.backup_plan: Not needed, real data access is achievable and strong here.

judge_qna.question: How does your system distinguish a routine industrial flare from an actual fire event at the same facility?
judge_qna.strong_answer: Walk through your specific discriminating features, thermal persistence patterns, intensity signatures, temporal behavior, that go beyond simple proximity to the facility.
judge_qna.follow_up: What real or realistic test case did you validate this discrimination against?

judge_qna.question: How did you validate your classifications are actually correct, not just plausible?
judge_qna.strong_answer: Describe your validation approach against known real events (documented industrial fires or known persistent flare locations) where ground truth is available.
judge_qna.follow_up: What's your system's behavior for a genuinely novel thermal source type it wasn't trained to recognize?
